content: Nearsightedness, or myopia, results in blurred vision when viewing distant objects. Various interventions have been studied to slow the progression of myopia in children, including the use of multifocal spectacles, contact lenses, and pharmaceutical agents. Spectacle Lenses Undercorrecting myopia slightly increased the progression of myopia in children. In two studies, children with undercorrected vision experienced an average progression of -0.15 diopters (D) more than those wearing fully corrected single vision lenses (SVLs). The axial length in the undercorrected group increased by 0.05 mm more than in the fully corrected group. Both findings were supported by low-certainty evidence. Multifocal lenses, such as bifocal spectacles or progressive addition lenses, showed a modest effect in slowing myopia progression. Children wearing multifocal lenses progressed 0.14 D less on average compared to those wearing SVLs. Axial elongation was also reduced by 0.06 mm in multifocal lens wearers. These results were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Studies on peripheral plus spectacle lenses compared to SVLs showed inconsistent results for refractive error and axial length outcomes, with low-certainty evidence. Contact Lenses Bifocal soft contact lenses (SCLs) showed little to no difference in refractive error progression compared to single vision SCLs. However, axial elongation was reduced by 0.11 mm in children wearing bifocal SCLs. These findings were supported by low-certainty evidence. Rigid gas permeable contact lenses (RGPCLs) showed inconsistent results in slowing myopia progression and no significant difference in axial elongation. The evidence for these findings was of very low certainty. Orthokeratology contact lenses were more effective than SVLs in slowing axial elongation, with a reduction of 0.28 mm. This was supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Spherical aberration SCLs showed no difference in myopia progression or axial elongation compared to single vision SCLs, based on low-certainty evidence. Pharmaceutical Agents Atropine eye drops were effective in reducing myopia progression. Children treated with atropine showed significantly less progression compared to those receiving placebo, with a mean difference of 1.00 D. Axial elongation was also reduced by 0.35 mm in atropine-treated children. These findings were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Pirenzepine gel and cyclopentolate eye drops also reduced myopia progression compared to placebo, with mean differences of 0.31 D and 0.34 D, respectively. Axial elongation was reduced by 0.13 mm in children treated with pirenzepine. These results were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Different doses of atropine (0.1%, 0.25%, and 0.5%) were more effective than tropicamide eye drops in slowing myopia progression, with mean differences ranging from 0.78 D to 1.01 D. However, axial length outcomes were not reported in this study, and the evidence was of low certainty. Systemic 7-methylxanthine had little to no effect on myopia progression or axial elongation compared to placebo, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Timolol eye drops did not significantly slow myopia progression compared to no treatment, with low-certainty evidence. Combination Treatments Atropine combined with multifocal spectacles was more effective than placebo combined with SVLs in reducing myopia progression by 0.78 D and axial elongation by 0.37 mm. These findings were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Atropine combined with multifocal spectacles was also more effective than cyclopentolate combined with SVLs, reducing myopia progression by 0.36 D. Bifocal spectacles combined with timolol drops showed a small or negligible effect compared to SVLs plus timolol drops, with a mean difference of 0.19 D. Tropicamide combined with bifocal spectacles showed no statistically significant differences compared to SVLs, but no quantitative results were reported. Adverse Effects No serious adverse events were reported across all interventions. However, children receiving antimuscarinic topical medications, such as atropine, were more likely to experience accommodation difficulties and the development of papillae and follicles compared to those receiving placebo. Conclusions Antimuscarinic topical medications, particularly atropine, are effective in slowing myopia progression in children. Multifocal lenses, including both spectacles and contact lenses, may provide a small benefit in reducing myopia progression. Orthokeratology contact lenses are effective in slowing axial elongation, although they are not designed to modify refractive error. Evidence supporting the use of RGPCLs and spherical aberration SCLs is of low or very low certainty.
